bivy.capacity: Numerous comfortable sites through the meadows and in the trees at their edge; this is the one place in the zone that will absorb several parties without crowding

itinerary: Typically done as an overnight or multi-day trip, with a high camp at Gardner Meadows (~10 miles in) or higher in Wolf Creek Basin (~6,200-6,400 ft) below the peak.

name: North Ridge
approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to Burlington, then WA-20 east through Marblemount, and turn onto Cascade River Road, following its paved-then-gravel surface about 21.7 miles to a small pullout at 3,200 ft that marks the unmaintained Boston Basin Trailhead (a different stop from the Eldorado trailhead about 2.5 miles down-road, and just before the road's end at Cascade Pass). From there a steep, unmaintained climbers' path follows the old Diamond Mine roadbed briefly before climbing hard, crossing several streams, and breaking above treeline (~5,300 ft) to reach the popular Boston Basin high camp around 6,400 ft — roughly 3-4 miles one-way with about 3,000-3,300 ft of elevation gain. From camp, West Ridge climbers continue cross-country over the glacier to a couloir that gains the ridge crest. Because Boston Basin is a high-demand cross-country camping zone in North Cascades National Park, overnight parties need a wilderness permit; a portion of peak-season (mid-May to mid-October) slots can be reserved in advance via Recreation.gov's early-access lottery, with the remainder issued as limited first-come, first-served walk-up permits. For this specific route: from Boston Basin high camp, a short approach up into the Forbidden Peak zone reaches this minor summit; North and South Ridge differ only in which side of the formation is climbed from the same camp.
descent: One 40-foot rappel from tower top, followed by down-climbing ridge.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are no longer free — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

itinerary: Day 1: Drive Cascade River Road to the Boston Basin trailhead (~3,200 ft); hike ~3-4 mi / ~3,000 ft gain to high camp (~6,400 ft). Day 2: Early start from camp, climb to the col and up the North Ridge to the tower and back (a half-day round trip is typical); hike out or stay a second night.

name: North Ridge - West Side
approach: Two primary approaches: (1) From the Cutthroat Lake trailhead on Highway 20, hike 1.8 miles with 500 feet elevation gain to Cutthroat Lake (4,800 ft). Continue another 3.7 miles with 1,800 feet elevation gain to Cutthroat Pass (6,800 ft), then follow the ridge crest south approximately 1 mile to the base of the North Ridge. (2) From Rainy Pass North trailhead (4,875 ft) on the PCT, hike about 1.5 miles north to just before Porcupine Creek (around 5,250 ft elevation), then ascend the ridge northeast toward Molar Tooth—approximately 2 miles with 2,300 feet elevation gain. The second gully provides a cleaner approach to the base of the north ridge and west rib. From the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead the round trip is roughly 4.5 miles with about 2,500 ft of gain.
descent: Descend via 3 rappels on the north ridge, or work southwest from the summit for an 80-foot rappel. Ensure solid anchor points as granite can be coarse and loose rock is prevalent. Exercise caution with rope management on descent.

bivy.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. It is the start for Cutthroat Wall and for the Cutthroat Lake trail toward Cutthroat Pass, and some parties sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
bivy.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
bivy.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
bivy.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

bivy.name: Cutthroat Lake basin, outside the quarter-mile closure
bivy.notes: The lake sits about 1.8 miles in with roughly 500 ft of gain, in the basin under the peak's north and east sides. It is a pleasant place to stage, but the quarter-mile closure exists because the shoreline was being loved to death and it is enforced rather than advisory. It does not serve Cutthroat Peak's south-side routes or the usual North Ridge approach: those start from a different trailhead, a long pullout on SR 20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, and cross State Creek into the basin south of the peak, so for them treat this as a rest-day or bad-weather option rather than a staging camp.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet stream are dependable all season. Treat or filter.
bivy.permit: No permit needed, but a hard rule applies: NO overnight camping within a quarter mile of Cutthroat Lake. Camp outside that radius and you are legal with no paperwork.
bivy.capacity: Limited and regulated — the usable ground is set back from the water, so realistically a handful of small parties

itinerary: Day 1: Drive to Cutthroat Lake trailhead or Rainy Pass. Hike to approach base (3-4 hours via Cutthroat Lake route, or 2-3 hours via PCT). Scout route and camp if needed. Day 2: Climb North Ridge - West Side (6-8 hours total from base for approach, climb, and descent). Conclude descent by mid-afternoon to avoid scrambling in dark.

waypoints.name: Cutthroat Lake basin, outside the quarter-mile closure

name: North Tower Ridge Route
approach: From Tiffany Springs Campground (6,760 ft), hike trail #373 east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass (7,150 ft, ~45 minutes). From the pass, either traverse south on the grassy east slope to the small cirque at the base of the North Face (7,360 ft) and climb the boulder field to the base of the climb (7,600 ft), or hike the trail on the north side of the ridge toward Little Tiffany Lake and drop down to the base from above (~30 minutes). Three driving approaches reach the Tiffany Springs trailhead: via Conconully/North Fork Salmon Creek and FR 39 (~21 mi, ~1 hr, rough road, 4WD recommended); via the South Fork/Baldy Pass (~30.6 mi, ~2 hr, 2WD-passable gravel); or via the Methow Valley (~26.5 mi, ~1 hr, 2WD gravel). An alternate trailhead at Freezeout Pass (via East Chewuch Rd/FR 37/FR 39 from Winthrop) also accesses the area and does not require a Northwest Forest Pass.
descent: Walk off the northwest ridge of Tiffany and then head northeast above Little Tiffany Lake to rejoin the main trail at Honeymoon Pass.

bivy.name: Tiffany Springs Campground
bivy.notes: This is the base for the north face and the trailhead in one, which is unusual and is what makes the face approachable at all: the walk to the bottom of the routes is under an hour, so a party can sleep at the car and still be climbing at first light without a bivouac. Trail 373 begins across the road from the campground and runs east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass at around 7,150 ft, from where the face is below you. The drive is the commitment. Three ways reach it and they are not equivalent: a narrow four-wheel-drive road over Lone Frank Pass from Conconully by the North Fork Salmon Creek, about twenty miles; a longer gravel road over Baldy Pass suited to two-wheel drive, about thirty; and a good two-wheel-drive gravel line from the Methow, north out of Winthrop on the Chewuch River road and then east and north on the 37 and 39, about twenty-six miles. Road 39 itself has not been graded in some time and is not recommended for low-clearance passenger cars. At this elevation the road holds snow late into the spring and can shut with the first serious autumn storm, so the usable window is short and both ends of it are worth checking rather than assuming.
bivy.water: No potable water and no tap — this is the single most important practical fact about the place, and its name is misleading. There is no piped supply, no water service and no rubbish service. Bring everything you need for drinking, cooking and washing, or plan to treat from Tiffany Lake, which is a short walk east on the trail and is the nearest dependable open water. In late summer this whole plateau is dry and what looks like a creek on a map may be nothing at all.
bivy.permit: National forest, outside designated wilderness, so there is no wilderness permit, no self-issue slip, no quota and no lottery — the opposite of the permit expectation a few miles west in the Pasayten. There is a small nightly fee at the campground and sites are first come, first served. Fire restrictions on this dry high plateau run through most of the summer and are commonly total bans, which given what has burned here recently should be treated as the default rather than the exception. Party size and stay limits are the usual forest ones.
bivy.capacity: A small primitive forest campground with a handful of sites, taking tents and modest vehicles. Trailers are not appropriate given the road. It is rarely full and it is the only organised camping anywhere near this face.

bivy.name: Tiffany Lake and Little Tiffany Lake
bivy.notes: Under a mile from the campground and directly on the approach, this is the camp for a party who would rather sleep on water than at a car, or who has arrived to find the campground full or closed. It is the last certain water before the face. The trail continues around the shore and climbs about six hundred feet to Honeymoon Pass, which is the gateway to the north side; parties leaving a second vehicle at the Freezeout Ridge roadhead can carry on over Whistler Pass at around 7,600 ft to the summit and descend the Freezeout trail, an open loop of some eleven miles that is the standard way to combine the walk-up with a look at the face. The burn is part of the landscape here. This trail travels through old fire scars that have opened the views and filled the ground with wildflower meadow, and the 2026 fire has added to that directly on this mountain — expect standing dead timber, no shade, and blowdown that changes with each windstorm. Do not pitch under dead trees in wind.
bivy.water: The lakes, and they are the dependable supply for the whole north side of this mountain — everything above them on the pass and the face runs on snowmelt and is dry once that has gone. Access to the water is easy from the trail. Treat it; these are shallow, warm, well-used lakes rather than cold alpine tarns.
bivy.permit: National forest, non-wilderness. No permit, no quota, no reservation, and no fee to camp at the lakes. A pass is not required to park at the campground trailhead across the road. Fire restrictions apply through the summer and are usually total bans; carry a stove. Camp back from the shoreline on existing bare ground, and note that this trail is open to horses and mountain bikes as well as walkers, so pitch clear of it.
bivy.capacity: A handful of informal spots around the shores, with the established ground at the north-west end of Little Tiffany Lake. Room for a party or two. Nothing developed and no toilet, and it sees family day-hiking traffic rather than climbers.

bivy.name: Honeymoon Pass
bivy.notes: The pass is where the trail crosses onto the north side and the face comes into view, and it is the tactical camp rather than the comfortable one. Its argument is a dawn start: from here the base of the routes is a short drop and a scramble rather than a walk from the road, which matters for the north-east couloir where the snow wants climbing early and matters much less for the rock, since the campground is under an hour away regardless. What you pay for the position is water and wind, in that order, and on a face this short the trade is rarely worth it — most parties are better off sleeping at the campground or the lake and walking in. Where it does earn its keep is for a party spending two days on the face, or one continuing over Whistler Pass to the summit and out by Freezeout Ridge. Nights are cold at this elevation from late August onward and there is no shelter at all if weather comes across the plateau.
bivy.water: None dependable. Snowmelt early in the season and nothing at all once it has gone. Everything is carried up from Tiffany Lake, six hundred feet and half a mile below, and the party that forgets this ends up walking back down for it in the evening. In the ice season it is a snow camp and you melt.
bivy.permit: National forest, non-wilderness — no permit, no quota, no reservation, no fee. Fire restrictions run through the summer and there is nothing to burn at this height in any case. The turf here is thin and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the meadow alone.
bivy.capacity: Open ground at the pass for a small party on gravel and thin turf. No established sites, no facilities and nothing to shelter behind. Windswept is the word most often used about this crest and it is accurate.

bivy.name: The talus and benches below the north face
bivy.notes: The routes start here and, on a face six hundred and fifty feet high forty-five minutes from a campground, essentially nobody sleeps here. It is written down because a party reading a list of camps should not be left to assume there is a bivouac at the base — there is not, and the answer to a late arrival is the campground, not the wall. The face itself is broken by several couloirs, aretes and vertical granite cliffs; the north-east couloir is the longest and most direct of the snow lines, on the left, and the tower at the right-hand end carries the rock routes, with the ridge line giving a vertical crack, a wide flaring chimney and long stretches of easy fourth-class scrambling on generally excellent rock. Because the snow goes soon after the roads become passable, the ice and couloir lines are a shoulder-season or winter objective and are reached by ski or snowmobile in that season rather than by driving to the campground. Treat the rock routes as the summer proposition and the couloirs as a separate trip requiring a separate approach.
bivy.water: Snowmelt off the couloirs early, and nothing whatsoever once that has gone. Given how early the snow leaves here after the roads open, that window is short. Carry water from the lakes; there is no source at the base of the face you should plan on.
bivy.permit: National forest, non-wilderness — no permit, no quota, no reservation. No fires: this is bare rock and talus with nothing to burn and fragile alpine ground around it. Standard leave-no-trace applies and human waste has to be carried out from the base of a face this small and this close to a road.
bivy.capacity: No established camping. There are boulder-field benches and scraps of flat ground at the foot of the wall where one or two people could put down a bag, and nothing more — this is a place to leave packs and gear up rather than a site, and it is recorded to say so rather than to invent one.

itinerary: Single long day: drive to Tiffany Springs Campground, hike ~45 min to Honeymoon Pass, traverse ~30 min to the base of the climb, climb the 6-pitch route (a few hours for a competent party), then walk off via the NW ridge and Little Tiffany Lake trail back to the car.

name: West Ridge
approach: Via Mosquito Lake Road (off SR 542 east of Deming) to a bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River, then Forest Road 38; park at the gate and continue roughly 5-6 miles with about 2,000-2,500 ft of gain on private-timberland logging roads (commonly covered by mountain bike) to reach the West Ridge climbers' path, which climbs through timber onto the ridge crest.
descent: Reverse the West Ridge (north of the crest near the false summits, south of it lower down); in early-mid season, some parties instead glissade/plunge-step the steep snow slopes on the north face.

bivy.name: Orsino Creek Basin
bivy.notes: This is the standard overnight camp for the west ridge of South Twin and the most useful water stop on the whole northwest approach. It is reached from the Dailey Prairie road system by crossing Orsino Creek and following a brushy old road that fades into a path through timber, then traversing up red talus past the ruins of an old cabin into the basin. From the camp a steep and thoroughly unpleasant slog up dirt, scree and talus gains an obvious notch on the west ridge at around five thousand two hundred feet. The ground is coarse and drains fast, so pitch on the flat gravel benches rather than hunting for soft ground. Fill everything here. Above this point the only water is snowmelt and glacier runoff, and in a dry August there may be none at all. Best from July through September; earlier the basin holds snow and the creek runs high and cold.
bivy.water: Orsino Creek, the most reliable water on the west side of the range. It is the last dependable source for the summits and for the higher camps, and it shrinks noticeably by late summer
bivy.permit: The basin sits close to the boundary between private timberland below and national forest wilderness above. Camping is legal on the forest side and not on the timber company side, and the line is not signed on the ground, so camp high in the basin rather than low. No overnight permit is currently required on the forest side; standard wilderness rules apply, including a party size limit of twelve. Campfires are a poor idea anywhere here and are banned outright on the private ground below; late summer fire restrictions are routine.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small dispersed sites among talus and heather; two to three tents

bivy.name: Dailey Prairie road end (staging and bike stash, not a camp)
bivy.notes: This old prairie is where the logging road system tops out and the climbers path to the west ridge of North Twin begins, roughly five miles and two thousand feet of road above the river bridge. Almost every party bikes to here and leaves the bike, which turns a brutal road walk into a fast coast on the way out. It reads like the obvious basecamp and it is not one: under the current landowner rules this ground is day use only, no camping and no fire, and vehicles must never block the road or the gate. Treat it as a staging point where you shoulder the pack for the last three thousand feet, and push on to the wilderness ground above if you want to sleep out. Snow lingers on the path above roughly four thousand feet well into early summer. The road is also subject to closure on short notice for active logging, quarry work or fire danger, and signs posting a closure have appeared with no warning.
bivy.water: None reliable at the prairie itself; carry what you need up from the valley
bivy.permit: Private industrial timberland. The gate at the Middle Fork river bridge is locked and keys are no longer issued for this northern entrance, so the road is foot and bicycle only. The landowner now runs a fee recreation permit covering this block of forestland, with a hard cap on the number of non-motorized permits issued, daylight-only entry of roughly an hour and a half either side of sunrise and sunset, no campfires at any time, and no camping. Ownership of these roads has changed hands more than once and the terms have changed with it, so confirm the current permit and gate situation with the landowner before you go rather than assuming older terms still apply.
bivy.capacity: Open ground with room for several parties, but overnight use is not permitted

bivy.name: Col between the Twins and the Sisters Glacier margin
bivy.notes: The saddle between North and South Twin sits at about five thousand eight hundred feet, with the Sisters Glacier, the largest ice in the range, on the northeast side of South Twin below it. Parties splitting the two Twins over two days camp in this area, and it is the natural high camp if you have come up from Orsino Creek Basin and want an early start on the traverse. The attraction is water: the glacier margin and the slabs below it carry running meltwater when nothing else on the crest does, and this is the last chance to fill before committing to the ridge south. It is a genuinely exposed spot with no shelter, and weather here can be far worse than in the valley. Later in the season the ice recedes, the slab runoff dries up, and the whole plan depends on melting snow instead. Check that there is still snow or ice water before relying on this camp in August or September.
bivy.water: Running water at the edge of the glacier and on the glacial slabs below the col in season. This is meltwater, so it flows on warm afternoons and can vanish on a cold morning or after the snow has gone
bivy.permit: National forest wilderness. Dispersed camping is legal with no overnight permit currently required, party size limited to twelve. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than on the thin heather, and pack out everything including waste. Campfires are inappropriate at this elevation and are usually prohibited under late season fire restrictions. A Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass is needed at the forest service trailheads on the southeast side.
bivy.capacity: Two or three small tents on gravel benches and slabs; exposed and windy

bivy.name: South Twin Sister summit bivies
bivy.notes: The highest summit in the range, somewhere between about six thousand nine hundred and seven thousand feet depending on which survey you believe, and the classic place to split the north to south traverse into two days. There are a number of flat gravel and rubble bivy spots scattered among the summit blocks, built up by parties over the years, and the view across to Mount Baker at dawn is the reason people do it. It is entirely waterless. The dunite the range is made of is dense and unfractured and sheds or swallows water rather than holding it, so there are no springs on the crest and no tarns near the summit; whatever you drink here you carried or melted. Exposed to everything, with no wind shelter beyond the blocks themselves. Reasonable from July into September once the snow has consolidated. Do not plan on finding snow to melt in a dry late summer.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow if there is any, otherwise carry every litre from Orsino Creek, the glacier margin or Green Creek
bivy.permit: National forest wilderness, dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve. No fires. The whole approach to this summit crosses private timberland where the current landowner permit applies, so the camp itself is legal while the walk to it may not be without the right paperwork.
bivy.capacity: Several small hand-built gravel platforms among the summit blocks; one or two tents plus tarps or bags

itinerary: A long day: reports give roughly 6-7 hours from trailhead to summit and 4-5 hours back down, on top of the logging-road approach.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Nooksack River Bridge / FR 38 Gate

name: Northeast Face Direct
approach: Mount Formidable is a deep objective on the Ptarmigan Traverse, reached from the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road. Take the maintained trail to Cascade Pass, then leave it and work across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow, up the Cache Glacier to Cache Col, and down the far side to camp at Kool-Aid Lake. From the lake continue south past Art's Knoll and cross the Red Ledge, then follow a rough path over meadow, snow and talus and drop several hundred feet to the bench on the Middle Cascade Glacier between its two icefalls. Cross the bench to the foot of the Formidable Glacier below the northeast face. Allow a full day or more from the car to Kool-Aid Lake and about three hours from camp to the base of the face. The descent is the South Route, back over the Spider-Formidable col and across the Middle Cascade Glacier and Red Ledge to camp. This is a multi-day glaciated objective that needs glacier travel skills.
descent: Descend the south/southeast side: scrambling, downclimbing, and rappels down to the Spider-Formidable col/crossover saddle, then reverse the Middle Cascade Glacier-Red Ledge approach back to camp.

bivy.name: Spider-Formidable Col
bivy.notes: The working base camp for both Spider Mountain and Mount Formidable, and the reason to know about it is that a party climbing either peak stops here while a party walking the traverse does not. The twin notches of the col divide the two mountains, and it is reached by crossing the upper Middle Cascade Glacier almost due south from the Red Ledge. Spider Mountain is climbed from here by its south gully, stepping onto the buttress to the east and finishing along a corniced east ridge, about nineteen miles round trip from the Cascade Pass trailhead. Formidable is the other direction, and its south scramble is only class 3 but is long, loose, exposed and hard to route-find, with a fatality on record; the same ground is the only practical descent. Estimates of the col's height run from roughly 6,600 to 7,400 feet. The descent off the south side toward Yang Yang can be very steep snow and parties have resorted to a hand line anchored on buried pickets.
bivy.water: Water trickles off the slabs beside the col through most of the climbing season, which is unusual for ground this high and is the main reason the col gets used as a base rather than just crossed. It is meltwater, so it weakens through August and can stop entirely in a light snow year, and there is nothing else until the lakes well below on either side.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit from the register at whichever trailhead you started from. Camp on snow, rock or bare slab rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere south of Cache Col. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: A small number of party-sized spots split between the west notch of the col and the ground above the east pass, on glacial slabs and snow. Two parties is comfortable, three is crowded, and there is no toilet.

bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake
bivy.notes: About one mile and 700 ft below Cache Col on a boot path. The usual first camp south of Cascade Pass and the base for Spider, Formidable and the south side of Magic.
bivy.water: The lake and snowmelt
bivy.permit: No permit required; the lake is outside the national park
bivy.capacity: Several tent sites on rock and heather benches around the lake

bivy.name: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
bivy.notes: The col is the gateway to everything here. From the Cascade Pass trail a boot path climbs south along the arm and onto the mellow Cache Glacier, which is corniced at the col early in the season and can need a careful step through. Parties who leave the car in the afternoon and lose the light on the climb sometimes stop here rather than commit to the awkward descending traverse beyond it, and parties coming back north at the end of a trip do the same. It is a fair-weather choice only: it is a high, open saddle with no shelter and no water, and in cloud the ground on both sides is easy to lose. Treat the elevation as approximate, since published figures for the col vary by a couple of hundred feet.
bivy.water: None at the col itself. Early in the season there are melt runnels on the shoulder below it; by August there is usually nothing, and parties either carry up from the Cascade Pass side or melt snow. This is the single most common reason people push on down to the tarn below instead of stopping here.
bivy.permit: This is the last ground on the park side, and the distinction decides which permit you need. A night at or above the col is inside North Cascades National Park and requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with part of the inventory reservable in advance and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage applies. One step south of the col you are in Glacier Peak Wilderness and a free self-issue register slip is all that is needed. Do not assume the wilderness self-issue covers a night at the col.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and a few rock benches on the shoulder below and at the col, room for one or two parties. Nothing built, no toilet, no windbreaks worth the name.

itinerary: Day 1: Cascade Pass trailhead to Kool-Aid Lake via Cascade Pass, Mixup Arm, Cache Glacier and Cache Col (~5 hrs); camp. Day 2: pre-dawn start, cross the Middle Cascade Glacier basin to the face base, climb the Direct Northeast Face (roughly 8-10.5 hrs from camp to summit), then descend via the South Route back to camp. Day 3: hike out to the trailhead.

name: Northeast Ridge (1963 Route)
approach: East/Northeast from Cascade Pass trailhead; descend and cross Cascade River, then approach the northeast face via C-J couloir
descent: Not specifically documented for this route; climbers on Johannesburg's other technical lines typically descend via "Doug's Direct" (traversing beneath Cascade Peak/the Triplets and over Mixup Peak's north ridge to Cache Glacier) or by rappelling the East Ridge back to the Cascade-Johannesburg col.

bivy.name: Johannesburg Camp
bivy.notes: A walk-in camp a short, steep and often slick few minutes above the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the road — not a drive-up campground, you carry everything in. It is the practical staging point for the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir, Cascade Peak, and any pre-dawn start where you want to be at the road end the night before. If it is full, Marble Creek and Mineral Park down the Cascade River Road are the car campgrounds, at the cost of driving the rough section twice.
bivy.water: A creek runs beside the sites and normally holds water through the season, being fed by drainage off the north side of Johannesburg Mountain rather than by a single small snowfield.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required even though the camp is minutes from the car; Cascade River Road permits are issued in person at Marblemount, part reservable on Recreation.gov and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.capacity: Three small primitive sites, so it is easily filled by one or two parties.

itinerary: Typically climbed over 2 days: Day 1 — approach from the Cascade Pass trailhead to a high bivy near the base of the Northeast Face/C-J couloir; Day 2 — climb the route to the summit, then descend via the East Ridge/C-J col and Doug's Direct back to the car (a long day; some parties add a 3rd day).

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead (end of Cascade River Road)

name: Northwest Face
approach: From the Dingford Creek Trailhead, where FR 56 is gated, follow Dutch Miller Gap Trail 1030 — the first 7.7 miles on the closed road to Hardscrabble Horse Camp — up the Middle Fork Snoqualmie valley toward Dutch Miller Gap, but do not go to the gap: leave the main Middle Fork Snoqualmie trail at a small steel bridge well before Dutch Miller Gap and cut cross-country south into Summit Chief Valley; the Northwest Face is visible on the east side of that valley — a distinctly different final leg than the Northeast Face's direct ridge approach.
descent: South along the connecting ridge to a pocket glacier, then glacier-polished slabs (trending climber's left) back to the ridge crest near 5,400'; 1-2 rappels, a goat-ledge traverse, and a forest descent return to camp.

bivy.name: Summit Chief Valley gravel flats
bivy.notes: Leave the Middle Fork trail at the small steel bridge and go cross-country south into Summit Chief Valley to a flat gravel wash below the face. The descent returns here.
bivy.water: Creek
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
bivy.capacity: A few low-impact sites on a gravel wash

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
bivy.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is gated at Dingford Creek, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. Burnt Boot Peak is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
bivy.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
bivy.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

itinerary: Day 1: Hike in from the Dingford Creek Trailhead (the closed road, then the trail to the steel bridge, plus additional cross-country travel) and establish camp at the ~4,650' gravel wash in Summit Chief Valley. Day 2: Climb the Northwest Face (Falcon Route) and descend via the south ridge/pocket glacier back to camp. Day 3: Hike out to the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Dingford Creek / Middle Fork Snoqualmie Trailhead
Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie

name: Summit Block — Northwest Edge Finish (variation)
approach: Same as Blue Glacier/East Face route approach until reaching the summit block base. Approach time is identical.
descent: Rappel from summit anchor down the northwest edge using a single rope to a belay ledge below, then downclimb and traverse to rejoin the standard descent route.

bivy.name: Glacier Meadows — the standard Blue Glacier base camp
bivy.notes: The standard base camp, roughly seventeen miles from the Hoh trailhead and the last established camp before the Blue Glacier — the park does not permit camping between here and the ice. From the meadows you climb the moraine, drop onto the glacier and work up past the Snow Dome to the summit rock, generally quoted as four to six miles and around 3,500 ft of gain each way, so most parties leave in the dark. accounts differ on the elevation, giving anything between about 4,200 and 4,400 ft, which matters only because published gain figures vary with it. A ranger station and pit toilets are here in season.
bivy.water: Reliable — meltwater creeks in the meadows; treat it, and expect it to run silty in hot weather
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, quota-limited, reserved on Recreation.gov. Bear canisters mandatory. Practically every party climbing Olympus wants this camp, so treat the permit as the crux of the trip rather than an afterthought.
bivy.capacity: A cluster of individual sites plus a group site, under a nightly quota; the single most contested permit on this approach

bivy.name: Lewis Meadows Camp, Hoh River trail
bivy.notes: The last low-elevation river camp on the Hoh before the trail leaves the valley floor, roughly ten miles in from the Hoh Rain Forest visitor centre. Climbers use it mainly to break the walk in when they cannot get a permit for Elk Lake or Glacier Meadows, or when a late start makes the full seventeen miles unrealistic. Because it sits at around a thousand feet in dense rainforest, it does nothing to shorten the climbing day — expect to still be four to five hours below the glacier the next morning. Pit toilet provided; bear canister required.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Hoh River runs alongside the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, reserved on Recreation.gov; this stretch of the Hoh is not one of the tightly capped camps, so it is usually easier to obtain than the two above it.
bivy.capacity: Several individual sites plus a designated group site; parties of seven or more must use the group site

bivy.name: Elk Lake Camp, Hoh River trail
bivy.notes: Elk Lake sits about fifteen miles up the Hoh, where the trail finally starts climbing hard, and it is the fallback base for parties who miss out on Glacier Meadows. From here the summit day is long — you still have the switchbacks to Glacier Meadows, the lateral moraine and the whole Blue Glacier ahead before any climbing starts. Some parties deliberately take Elk Lake on the walk in and Glacier Meadows on the walk out, which spreads the permit demand across two nights. Pit toilet provided; food must be in an approved canister.
bivy.water: Reliable — Elk Lake itself, plus creeks nearby; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required and this is an explicitly quota-limited camp — reserve on Recreation.gov well ahead. Summer-season reservations open in mid-April and the popular Hoh camps can be gone the same morning.
bivy.capacity: A small handful of individual sites; it fills every summer night in season

bivy.name: Snow Dome / Caltech Rocks high bivy, on the Blue Glacier
bivy.notes: Strong parties skip the pre-dawn start from Glacier Meadows by carrying a light camp onto the ice, either into the rocks below the Snow Dome or onto the dome near the old weather station. It turns a brutal summit day into a short one and puts you above most of the morning cloud, at the cost of a much heavier pack up the moraine and a night with no liquid water. This is glacier camping — crevasse hazard, wind, and no shelter — so it suits parties already competent on the Blue Glacier rather than as a way of making the route easier. The exact spots shift year to year as the ice and moraine change, so no single elevation is recorded.
bivy.water: Snow and glacier melt only; you are melting or filtering meltwater, and there is no running source you can count on
bivy.permit: Covered by an Olympic Wilderness Permit, but note that camping is NOT allowed between Glacier Meadows and the Blue Glacier — these sites are on the glacier side of that closure. Human waste must be packed out in blue bags, and bear canisters still apply.
bivy.capacity: Informal — a scatter of tent platforms in the rock bands and on the dome itself; no designated sites and no facilities

itinerary: Same as Blue Glacier standard route; variation only on summit block.

waypoints.name: Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center / Hoh River Trailhead
Lewis Meadows Camp, Hoh River trail
Elk Lake Camp, Hoh River trail

name: One Piece at a Time
approach: This is a distinct approach from the one used for Cutthroat Peak, which starts from an unmarked highway pullout about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass with no maintained trail. For Cutthroat Wall, start on the maintained Cutthroat Creek Trail #483 from the Cutthroat Trailhead kiosk. After a short distance on the main trail, leave it via a cairned path that cuts into the forest, then follow cairns and a climbers' path (roughly 1.5-2 miles, 45 min-2 hrs total) through brush and talus, trending toward the buttress, to reach the base of Cutthroat Wall.
descent: Three 60m rappels from trees, starting slightly uphill of the P5 belay.

bivy.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. It is the start for Cutthroat Wall and for the Cutthroat Lake trail toward Cutthroat Pass, and some parties sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
bivy.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
bivy.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
bivy.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground to Washington Pass, on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek six or seven miles east of the pass, just past the turn for the Cutthroat Creek road. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
bivy.water: No drinking water at Lone Fir. Early Winters Creek runs through the campground and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: 27 sites, tents and small RVs

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
bivy.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
bivy.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
bivy.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
bivy.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

bivy.name: Cutthroat Wall base terrace
bivy.notes: The approach leaves the old roadbed a quarter mile from the trailhead at cairns, then climbs left through trees and light brush to a flat bench beneath the west-northwest-facing granite. Most parties do these routes car-to-car in a day, so a bivy here is for a late start or a two-day plan rather than standard practice. The wall faces away from morning sun, which makes an early camp less useful than it looks on the map. The crag is sometimes catalogued under Little Liberty Bell, which is the same approach and the same ground.
bivy.water: No water on the terrace itself. Fill in Cutthroat Creek low on the approach and carry it up.
bivy.permit: None — dispersed national forest camping, no permit and no quota.
bivy.capacity: A small flat area under the cliff; room for one or two parties at most

itinerary: Full day: early start, approach to base (roughly 1-2 hrs from the trailhead), 6 pitches (4-6 hrs), then three rappels to descend (about 1-1.5 hrs).

waypoints.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby

name: Painted Traverse
approach: From the North Fork Sauk trailhead, the Red Mountain (Painted Mountain Lookout) Trail branches left about 100 yards in and climbs about a mile to the old lookout site near 3,100 ft. Beyond it an unmaintained climber's path goes straight up the slope with almost no switchbacks, including a short cliff band that needs class 3 scrambling, and continues steeply to the summit of Painted Mountain. Expect close to 5,000 ft of gain in under three miles.
itinerary: Very fit, fast parties do it in a single long day starting before dawn; most parties take two to three days, camping near Black Mountain where water is most reliable.

name: Plan 9 from Outer Space
approach: From the Goodell Creek group-camp trailhead near Newhalem, walk the overgrown Goodell Creek roadbed for about 4 miles to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing, then climb the Terror Creek climbers' path. The Blob stands above Crescent Creek Basin, so from the Terror Creek side you must cross the Barrier, the loose, brushy ridge dividing the Terror Creek drainage from Crescent Creek; it can be crossed low or high from Terror Basin. Descend into Crescent Creek Basin and camp within reach of the Himmelhorn and the Blob, then scramble to the base of the south buttress. This is a serious multi-day expedition approach requiring a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, off-trail routefinding through brush and talus, and glacier/snow travel gear.
descent: Traverse the Blob's summit ridge north to the Blob/Terror col, then make 2 rappels from webbing anchors into the notch below.

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is not on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is walk-up only — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is legally awkward: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

itinerary: Typically done as part of a multi-day Southern Pickets trip: Day 1, backpack in via the Goodell Creek roadbed and Terror Creek climbers' path to a high camp near the Barrier or in Terror Basin; Day 2, cross the Barrier into Crescent Creek Basin and establish camp within striking distance of the Himmelhorn/Blob area; Day 3, climb Plan 9 from Outer Space and return to camp via the Blob/Terror col rappels; Day 4, hike out.

name: Playing Not Spraying
approach: The Silver Horn is a sub-summit on the east ridge of Silver Star Mountain, east of the main summit, and both of its routes are on the clean white granite of its south face. That face is not reached from the Wine Spires pullout or Burgundy Col, which serve the other side of the crest. Instead, walk the Cedar Creek Trail from its trailhead at the end of FR 5310-200, off SR-20 about half a mile east of the Klipchuck Campground turnoff. After roughly five miles, turn off to the right below the old burn and follow a rough path up the right-hand side of the creek that drains the south side of the Silver Horn. Meadows at about 6,200 ft give good camping below the face.
descent: Rappel the SE side of the peak.

bivy.name: Meadows below the Silver Horn's south face
bivy.notes: The camp for both routes on the south face, in the meadows at about 6,200 ft where the creek draining the Silver Horn's south side opens out below the white granite. Reached from the Cedar Creek Trailhead: about five miles up the Cedar Creek Trail, then right below the old burn onto a rough path up the right-hand side of that creek. This is not the Wine Spires pullout or Burgundy Col — those serve the other side of the crest and do not reach this face. It is a rarely visited corner with no established climbers' camp and little traffic, so expect to pick your own spot on the meadow.
bivy.water: The creek the approach path follows is the water source on the way up. How late in the season it still runs at the meadows is not recorded, so carry enough capacity for a dry camp late in a dry year.
bivy.permit: No reservation, no quota and no overnight permit; national forest dispersed-camping rules apply. A Northwest Forest Pass, an Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking at the Cedar Creek Trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Open meadow with room for a few tents; no established sites

itinerary: Day 1: Drive to the Cedar Creek Trailhead, hike ~5 miles up the Cedar Creek Trail, leave the trail below the old burn, and work up along the south-face drainage to camp in the meadows at ~6,200 ft. Day 2: Climb the 8-pitch route, rappel the SE side back to camp, and hike out via Cedar Creek Trail.
